idiom_name: facade module: public header plus one function per application operation
implementation_notes: C has no classes, DI or annotations, so the service layer is a facade module: one public header declares the application's operations over an opaque handle, and the implementation file writes each operation as an orchestration script that calls the domain and data-access modules and owns the transaction. A single begin/commit/rollback pair - for example sqlite3_exec("BEGIN") / "COMMIT", or a db_begin()/db_commit() wrapper around the driver - replaces the container-managed transaction of the classic form, and there is no dispatcher, so the 'layer supertype' becomes a struct of function pointers passed to every operation. The hand-written structure is still justified when several front ends (CLI, daemon, test harness) must share one operation set; for a single small tool that calls the data layer directly, the module is ceremony.
pitfalls: Transaction state belongs to the connection: a service function that returns early without commit or rollback leaves the connection inside an open transaction and poisons every later caller.
There is no dynamic dispatch, so every client links the same header and any signature change breaks them at link time - version the operation set, not the struct layout.
Exposing the db handle in the public header lets callers run SQL around the boundary and bypass the transaction the service is supposed to own.
